newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russian draftees look up to Western heroes - general.
newsitem.headline: Russian draftees look up to Western heroes - general.

text.p: Young Russians called up for national service are increasingly unhealthy, unpatriotic, uneducated and likely to dodge the draft, a general in charge of conscription said in a newspaper interview published on Wednesday.

General Mikhail Klishin, suggesting draftees are more likely to model themselves on the all-American Rambo than on Russian heroes, revealed yet more problems for Russia's armed forces as reforms remain on hold while President Boris Yeltsin is ill.
Klishin said 37,000 young men had dodged last autumn's call-up compared with 44,000 in the whole of 1993, 16,000 in 1991 and only 443 in Soviet times in 1985.
"The situation has to be qualified as critical, as legal nihilism," he told the defence ministry newspaper Krasnaya Zvezda (Red Star).

"It is not by chance that fighting heroes from Western cinema serve as models for many and that only a few can remember the Russian warriors who won victories in the name of the defence of the Fatherland. Even fewer want to be like these heroes."
Klishin, head of a department in the General Staff responsible for conscription, said one in three young men called up was not fit to serve for medical reasons.
Five years ago, as the Soviet era ended, just one in five had been deemed unfit and the comparative figure for 1985 was a mere one in 20. The call-up starts at the age of 18.

Among the main illnesses were difficulties related to internal organs, psychologcial disorders and problems with the nervous system. The number of youngsters with syphilis was 11 times higher than in 1985.
Klishin said he was alarmed that youngsters being called up were also now less well educated.
"This causes concern for the future of the army and, on a broader scale, the intellectual future of society," he said.
Asked about crime among young servicemen, he said police had found that many of those who committed crimes used drugs and alcohol regularly.
Many who answered the call-up did not see any need for national service and were not interested in or knowledgeable about Russia's history, literature or military studies.
"Among the youngsters called up there is a devaluation of the significance of military service and an erosion of patriotic values and ideals," Klishin said.
He said his department had received only 25 percent of the the money needed for the autumn call-up. "There is a lack of money for literally everything," he said.

Klishin's comments were only the latest to paint a picture of faded glory in the army, once the pride of Soviet society but now short of money and disillusioned by the failure to smash a few thousand separatist fighters in the Chechen conflict.
Yeltsin and the government have promised major reforms, including reducing the size of the armed forces and making the army fully professional by around the year 2005.

But the reforms have been stalled by Yeltsin's almost constant absence from the Kremlin with health problems since his re-election last July, a lack of funds and disputes over how the reforms should be carried out.

Klishin said a radical overhaul was needed to put matters right with conscription. But his chances of achieving his aim to "make the call-up, like never before, a festive occasion for all our lads", appear slim.
